A matrix equation AX = B solves one system for each column of B, yielding X = A B. For
XA = B the inverse must instead multiply on the right. Explicit inversion can be slower than
elimination, but the formula is useful for parameter dependence and conceptual questions. If a
square matrix is singular, no right-hand side has a unique solution.
−1
For two-by-two matrices, tr(A ) = tr A/ det A, where trace means the sum of diagonal entries.
A small nonzero determinant can make the inverse large; as matrices approach a singular limit,
a small right-hand side need not give a small solution. Inverse action can also be computed
from known images by linearity.

The equations tx + y = 1, x + ty = 1 have a unique real solution for which t?
(A) t ̸= 0 (B) t ̸= 1 (C) t ̸= −1 (D) t ̸= ±1 (E) Every real t

solution.text:
2
The coefficient determinant is t − 1. It is nonzero exactly for t ̸= ±1. At t = 1 there are
infinitely many solutions, while at t = −1 the two equations contradict each other.
